subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which EM wave is used in medical X-ray imaging of bones?
questions.explain: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by denser bone, producing a shadow image. They are ionising, so doses are kept low and staff are shielded.

questions.q: Roughly what is the radius of an atom?
questions.explain: An atom has a radius of about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. The nucleus is far smaller, roughly 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m, around ten thousand times smaller than the atom.

questions.q: What is the first stage in the life cycle of a star?
options: A nebula (cloud of dust and gas) collapsing into a protostar
questions.explain: A star begins as a nebula. Gravity pulls the dust and gas together to form a protostar, which heats up until nuclear fusion of hydrogen begins, forming a main sequence star.

questions.q: Which use is correctly matched to its EM wave?
options: Gamma rays – sterilising medical equipment and treating cancer
questions.explain: Gamma rays are used to sterilise equipment and to kill cancer cells. Microwaves carry satellite/phone signals, radio waves broadcast, and infrared is used for heating and remote controls.

questions.q: In the nuclear symbol of an atom, what does the bottom (smaller) number represent?
questions.explain: The bottom number is the atomic (proton) number — the number of protons. The top number is the mass number (protons + neutrons).

questions.q: A nucleus undergoes alpha decay. How do its mass number and atomic number change?
options: Mass number stays the same, atomic number +1
questions.explain: An alpha particle is ⁴₂He, so the nucleus loses 4 from its mass number and 2 from its atomic number.

questions.q: Which type of electromagnetic wave is used for broadcasting television and radio signals over long distances?
questions.explain: Radio waves are used for TV and radio broadcasting. They have long wavelengths and can be transmitted, received and reflected over long distances.

questions.q: Compared with radio waves, gamma rays have a:
questions.explain: Gamma rays sit at the high-frequency end of the spectrum, so they have a much shorter wavelength and higher frequency than radio waves (frequency and wavelength are inversely related for a fixed speed).

questions.q: Where are elements heavier than iron formed?
options: In the cores of low-mass main sequence stars
questions.explain: Fusion in stars produces elements up to iron. Elements heavier than iron are formed in the huge energies of a supernova explosion, which then scatters them into space.

questions.q: What is the difference between irradiation and contamination?
options: Irradiation means being exposed to radiation from a source; contamination means having radioactive atoms on or inside an object
Contamination only happens with gamma radiation
Irradiation means a radioactive material gets onto or into an object; contamination means being exposed to radiation from a source
They are exactly the same thing
questions.explain: Irradiation is exposure to radiation from an external source (the object does not become radioactive). Contamination is when radioactive atoms get onto or inside an object, which then continues to emit radiation.

questions.q: Radioactive decay is described as a random process. What does this mean?
options: The source decays at a steady, predictable rate per nucleus
Decay only happens when the source is disturbed
All nuclei decay at exactly the same time
It is impossible to predict which nucleus will decay next or when
questions.explain: Decay is random: you cannot predict which nucleus will decay or when. A Geiger–Müller tube can measure the overall count-rate, but individual decays are unpredictable.

questions.q: What does CMBR (cosmic microwave background radiation) provide evidence for?
questions.explain: The cosmic microwave background radiation is low-level microwave radiation found across all of space. It is best explained as the leftover 'afterglow' of the Big Bang, which only the Big Bang theory predicts.

questions.q: Which EM wave is used in fibre-optic communications and in TV remote controls?
questions.explain: Infrared is used to carry signals along optical fibres and in remote controls. It is also emitted by warm objects and used in thermal imaging.

questions.q: Which use is correctly matched to the EM wave?
options: Microwaves – cooking food and satellite communications
questions.explain: Microwaves are used for cooking and satellite/mobile communications. Infrared is used in remote controls and heating; gamma rays sterilise equipment and treat cancer; UV causes tanning.

questions.q: Which material is needed to absorb (significantly reduce) gamma radiation?
options: Thick lead or several metres of concrete
questions.explain: Gamma is the most penetrating: paper stops alpha, a few mm of aluminium stops beta, but gamma needs thick lead or metres of concrete to reduce it significantly.

questions.q: Which EM wave is used to take images of broken bones and is ionising?
questions.explain: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by bone, producing medical images. They are ionising, so exposure is kept as low as possible.

questions.q: Why should people limit their exposure to ultraviolet radiation from the Sun or sunbeds?
options: UV is ionising and can damage skin cells, causing sunburn and increasing skin cancer risk
UV cools the skin too much
questions.explain: Ultraviolet is ionising enough to damage skin cells and DNA, leading to sunburn, premature ageing and an increased risk of skin cancer; sunscreen and limiting exposure reduce the risk.

questions.q: What is meant by the half-life of a radioactive isotope?
options: The time for the activity to double
Half the age of the sample
The time for the number of undecayed nuclei to halve
The time for the source to completely decay
questions.explain: Half-life is the time taken for the number of undecayed nuclei in a sample to halve (equivalently for its activity/count-rate to halve).

questions.q: Which EM wave is used in medicine to form images of bones?
questions.explain: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by denser bone, so they are used to image bones and detect fractures. They are ionising, so exposure is kept low.

questions.q: When a nucleus emits a beta-minus particle, how does its atomic number change?
questions.explain: In beta-minus decay a neutron becomes a proton (plus the emitted electron), so the mass number is unchanged but the atomic number increases by 1.

questions.q: Put the correct end-of-life path for a HIGH-mass star in order.
options: Red super giant → supernova → neutron star or black hole
Red super giant → white dwarf → neutron star
Red giant → white dwarf → black hole
questions.explain: A high-mass star becomes a red super giant, then explodes as a supernova. The remaining core becomes a neutron star, or a black hole if the star was massive enough.

questions.q: Which type of nuclear radiation is the most strongly ionising but the least penetrating?
questions.explain: Alpha radiation is the most strongly ionising but least penetrating — it is stopped by a sheet of paper or a few cm of air.
